---
title: "Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

This is the 12-bar blues for instruments that play one note at a time: violin, saxophones,
and anything else with a single line. It starts with one note per chord and ends with a
line that spells out a jazz blues. You need to be able to read notes in your instrument's
range. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see
[Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues](blues-changes.qmd).

**Choose your instrument first.** The **Instrument** menu in the strip at the bottom
transposes the page. Violinists leave it on concert pitch. Alto and tenor players choose
their saxophone, and every chart and line of notation is then written in *their* key, while
the band plays in the concert key shown beside it. A B♭ tenor and an E♭ alto reading this
page at the same time see different notes and sound the same ones.

**How to use the page.** Every step is a twelve-bar line. Under each note is the name of
its place in the chord at that moment: R for the root, then 3, 5, ♭7. Press **▶ Play**
beside the notation to hear the line alone, or **▶ Play with the band** to hear it over the
rhythm section, where the piano plays it. Tick **Leave out the melody** to play it yourself.
The note that is sounding lights up in the notation either way.

Sections 1 to 6 build the skills. Section 7 puts them to work on a tune, Oscar Pettiford's
*Blues in the Closet*. If you would rather start with the tune, go there first and come
back.

## 1. The roots

The **root** is the note a chord is named after. A blues has three chords and three roots.
Play each one as a long note and count the bars: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V,
IV, I, I.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="roots"></div>

A bass player would play these notes. Playing them yourself is the quickest way to hear
where the form turns.

## 2. Chord tones, and the 3rd and 7th

A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the **root**, the
**3rd**, the **5th** and the **7th**. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a
flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a *dominant* seventh chord. Here are the four notes of each
chord, played up from the root.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tones"></div>

The 3rd and the 7th are the **guide tones**. They are the two notes that tell a listener
which chord this is, and they are the notes a good melody leans on.

### Where the flat 7 comes from

Why is the 7th of these chords called *flat*? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to
hear each line. The explanation follows the key and instrument chosen in the strip at the
bottom.

<div class="bl-scale"></div>

## 3. Guide-tone lines

Play only a guide tone of each chord, and at each change move to the *nearest* guide tone
of the new chord. The line barely moves: when I7 goes to IV7 the 3rd falls a half step and
becomes the ♭7th of the new chord. One note per bar, and the whole harmony of the blues is
in it.

Starting on the 3rd:

<div class="bl-step" data-part="guide3"></div>

Starting on the 7th. Two players can take one line each.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="guide7"></div>

## 4. Guide tones in rhythm

The same notes become a background figure when they are given a rhythm. This one is the
Charleston: a note on beat 1 and another on the "and" of 2. A horn section plays exactly
this kind of thing behind a soloist.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="rhythm"></div>

## 5. A riff

A riff is a short figure repeated through the form and adjusted to fit the chords. This one
is the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 5th of the home chord. Over the IV chord only its first note
changes: it drops a half step, which makes it the ♭7th of IV. Over the V chord the whole
figure moves up to that chord.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="riff"></div>

Look at the names under the notes in bars 5 and 6. The fingers play almost the same thing,
and every note has a new job.

## 6. The jazz blues

The last line of a jazz blues is a **two-five**: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8
to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of
[the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd)). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord, with a
minor 3rd. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide-tone line steps down: the 7th of each chord
falls to the 3rd of the next.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="guide3" data-chart="jazz"></div>

The chord tones of the same chorus:

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tones" data-chart="jazz"></div>

## 7. The tune: Blues in the Closet

Oscar Pettiford wrote this blues in the early 1950s. It is a *riff blues*: one two-bar idea,
played three times over the twelve bars. Learn the first two bars and you know nearly all
of it.

<div class="bl-step" data-chart="closet" data-tune="closet"></div>

### How it is built

- **Four notes.** The whole melody uses the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. Look
  at the names under bars 1 and 2: R, 3, R, 4, 3, R.
- **Three lines.** Bars 1 to 4, 5 to 8 and 9 to 12 are the same riff. Each ends on a long
  note, which is where the rhythm section answers.
- **Notes that arrive early.** Several notes are tied across the barline. They are played
  an eighth note *before* the beat and held into the next bar. Clap the rhythm before you
  play it. These early notes are what make the riff swing.

### The one note that changes

In bars 5 and 6 the riff's second note is a half step lower than it was in bars 1 and 2.
It is the only accidental in the tune. Over the home chord that note was the **3rd**. The
IV chord has that pitch a half step lower, as its **♭7th**, so the melody moves with the
chord. In bar 7 the home chord returns and so does the original note. This is the sound of
a blues going to IV, and the melody tells you the chord has changed without any help from
the band.

Hear that move by itself. This is the guide-tone line from section 3 on the tune's changes.
Play it, then play the tune again and listen for the same half step inside the riff.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="guide3" data-chart="closet"></div>

### The last line

Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five (ii7 then V7) instead of V then IV. The melody does not
change at all, but look at the names under it: the same pitches are now the 9th and ♭7th of
the ii chord. A riff this simple fits because every one of its notes belongs to the key.

The roots of the tune, to learn where the chords fall:

<div class="bl-step" data-part="roots" data-chart="closet"></div>

### Practising it

1. Sing the riff with the band before you play it.
2. Play bars 1 and 2 alone until the tied notes sit right. Use **▶ Play** beside the
   notation to check yourself.
3. Play the whole tune with **Leave out the melody** ticked.
4. Change the concert key. A riff you can play in three keys is a riff you know.

When the tune is secure, go on to [the improvising lesson](blues-improv.qmd), which uses
this melody as its starting point.

## Where to go next

- Change the concert key and play every step again. F, B♭, C and G are the keys a blues is
  most often called in.
- Loop a chorus with the melody left out and make up your own line from the chord tones,
  landing on a guide tone at each change.
- Take a chorus from [the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd) and write its guide-tone line.
